title: Flip

jokes.text: Larry's farewell speech opens with dignified talk of 'giving somebody else a turn' — then reveals the real reason: 'Having run out of fresh, exciting, new ideas to bring you myself'
jokes.setup: Larry begins a grandiose, self-congratulatory farewell monologue in the vein of a statesman retiring from public life
jokes.punchline: He casually admits mid-speech that he's simply run out of ideas — puncturing his own dignity completely
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Larry Sanders — the character's grandiosity and self-awareness exist simultaneously. He positions his retirement as noble generosity, then almost parenthetically admits the actual mundane reason. The structure is elegant: build up the pomp, then deflate it with one clause. Character-specific because this particular flavor of oblivious narcissism is uniquely Larry's.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Having run out of fresh, exciting, new ideas to bring you myself

jokes.text: 'And who knows? Some day I may reenter the lists with a new saber, neither broken nor bent, and plow up the field all over again.'
jokes.setup: Larry is delivering what sounds like a sincere, eloquent farewell
jokes.punchline: He can't resist leaving the door open — his 'goodbye' is already hedged with a comeback fantasy, undermining the whole valedictory premise
jokes.explanation: The metaphor is slightly overwrought ('saber,' 'plow up the field') which is part of the joke — Larry's self-image is epic and pompous. But this is a slower burn; the comedy is in recognizing the character's inability to truly let go, which compounds nicely as the episode progresses.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Some day I may reenter the lists with a new saber, neither broken nor bent, and plow up the field all over again

jokes.text: Larry asks if he should mention God in his final goodbye. Artie responds: 'Well, hell, we plugged everybody else on the planet. Let's give the deity his due.'
jokes.setup: Larry sincerely wonders if invoking God in his farewell would be appropriate
jokes.punchline: Artie reframes it as just another plug in a long list of plugs — putting God on the same commercial level as network guests
jokes.explanation: Artie's line is sharp and perfectly economical. The joke works on two levels: it's a wry take on the hollow showbiz 'thank you God' convention, AND it's completely in character for the pragmatic, seen-it-all producer. 'Let's give the deity his due' has a dry musicality that makes it quotable. Near-perfect line delivery premise.

dialogue.line: Come on, blanket. We're going to go home

jokes.text: After Hank's overwrought speech about what the last 10 years mean to Larry, ending with '...a gift to a man by the name of Hank Kingsley' — followed by sighs and 'Ok? Ok.'
jokes.setup: Hank appears to be giving a moving speech on Larry's behalf about the gift of the last decade
jokes.punchline: He pivots the entire tribute to being about himself — 'a man by the name of Hank Kingsley' — then the awkward 'Ok? Ok.' exchange reveals Larry's exhausted tolerance
jokes.explanation: Hank's self-insertion is the character's defining trait executed beautifully. He literally makes Larry's farewell about himself. The 'Sighs... Ok? Ok.' beat is pure Larry Sanders Show — the comedy isn't in the line but the aftermath, the resigned acceptance. Character integration is near-perfect: this exact move is impossible coming from any other character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You think I should mention God? Well, hell, we plugged everybody else on the planet. Let's give the deity his due

jokes.text: Beverly is crying, and the staff is exasperated. Hank: 'Come on. You're gonna get me started, and, believe me, nobody needs to see that.' Then immediately: 'You should've seen me at the end of Titanic. You think those people in the water were wailing?'
jokes.setup: Hank positions himself as someone who must stay strong and not cry — implying stoicism
jokes.punchline: He immediately undermines this by volunteering that he was MORE hysterical than drowning Titanic passengers — a wildly disproportionate comparison
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. The two-beat structure is excellent: first Hank establishes himself as the voice of restraint, then immediately obliterates that persona with a deeply specific and absurd self-comparison to Titanic drowning victims. 'You think those people in the water were wailing?' is the kind of disproportionate image that sticks. It's pure Hank — self-aggrandizing even in vulnerability, wildly specific, delivered with total conviction.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: The last 10 years have been your glorious gift to the people of this country. But they've also have been a gift... to a man by the name of Hank Kingsley

jokes.text: Cut from the emotional farewell rehearsal to a lone voice saying: 'Fucking bunch of bullshit.'
jokes.setup: The preceding scene is all tearful, emotional, overwrought farewell sentiment
jokes.punchline: A hard cut and a single perfectly timed expletive deflates all of it
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words after a sustained emotional buildup. The Larry Sanders Show specialized in this kind of puncturing cut. It scores slightly lower on character integration since the speaker is unidentified, but as a structural joke it's executed with precision. The audience earns the release.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I think the hormones from the baby... You should've seen me at the end of Titanic. You think those people in the water were wailing?

jokes.text: Phil asks if he can take the giant 'LARRY' letters from the set — but clarifies: not all of them, just the ones that spell his friend 'Ray'
jokes.setup: Phil asks to take the letters, which seems like a sentimental request
jokes.punchline: He reveals he just wants to spell his buddy's name on a lawn as a prank — and only needs R, A, Y — an oddly specific and completely trivial scheme
jokes.explanation: The joke has charm — the specificity of the prank (spelling 'ray' on a lawn, imagining the friend opening the blinds) is delightfully mundane against the grandiose backdrop of the final show. Works as character-level observational humor about the lower-tier crew members who aren't caught up in the legend of it all.

dialogue.line: [Sighs] Fucking bunch of bullshit

jokes.text: Larry tells Phil the letters are owned by the network, then adds: 'But if it was up to me, seriously, you would not get them.'
jokes.setup: Larry appears to be giving Phil the polite corporate excuse for why he can't have the letters
jokes.punchline: He pivots to make it personal — he genuinely wouldn't give them anyway — adding the unnecessary 'seriously' for extra deadpan weight
jokes.explanation: The 'but if it was up to me, seriously' turn is a great Larry moment — he has to add the personal pettiness even when the corporate excuse would have sufficed. The 'seriously' lands perfectly; it signals he's not joking about his own pettiness. Classic Larry self-sabotage.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I have this buddy Ray... I could take the letters that just spell his name, and then I could put them on the lawn of his house

jokes.text: Phil points out the letters will be in a dumpster after the show. Larry replies: 'You know tomorrow night after the show, yeah? You're fired. But for the last time, so celebrate.'
jokes.setup: Phil argues the network won't care about the letters anyway
jokes.punchline: Larry fires him with cheerful framing — 'for the last time, so celebrate' — turning a termination into a gift
jokes.explanation: Tight, dark, and characterful. 'For the last time, so celebrate' is the kind of casually cruel Larry Sanders line that earns genuine laughter — he's not even being mean, just efficient. The 'celebrate' pivot is the key word. Very quotable micro-moment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: But if it was up to me, seriously, you would not get them

jokes.text: Larry says 'Don't ask me for the couch' as Phil exits — preemptively denying another request with deadpan resignation
jokes.setup: Phil has already asked for set pieces (the letters). The firing has just happened.
jokes.punchline: Larry anticipates the next ask — 'Don't ask me for the couch' — suggesting a whole pattern of people trying to strip the set as mementos
jokes.explanation: Quick and clean. Works as a miniature callback/running gag — people raiding the set — and adds texture to the chaotic final-day vibe. Not a heavy hitter but efficiently placed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You know tomorrow night after the show? You're fired. But for the last time, so celebrate

jokes.text: Larry responds to the 'wedding vows' comparison: 'I think you should wear a veil. I think we should come down the aisle together, maybe in white.'
jokes.setup: Hank proposes their thank-yous be like wedding vows
jokes.punchline: Larry plays along with the metaphor in the driest possible way, extending it to veil and white dress — simultaneously mocking Hank and the absurdity of the conversation
jokes.explanation: Good Larry move — he plays the absurdity straight rather than deflecting it. The extension of the metaphor ('maybe in white') has the right dry quality. Lands as a callback escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Don't ask me for the couch

jokes.text: Hank's demands include: 'Don't lump me in with those fucking craft service retards.'
jokes.setup: Hank is negotiating the terms of his on-air thank-you
jokes.punchline: His contempt extends to the craft service staff — the lowest-tier workers — revealing the precise hierarchy of his ego and his paranoia about being lumped in with anyone beneath him
jokes.explanation: Deeply Hank. The specificity of 'craft service' — the absolute bottom of the showbiz hierarchy — shows the writers know exactly how to calibrate his insecurity. The slur dates the episode and is uncomfortable, but the character logic is airtight.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I think my thank-you should not come directly after yours, 'cause that would sound tit for tat

jokes.text: Larry asks who they have for the show. Artie says 'Carol Burnett.' Larry: 'Think she'll cry?'
jokes.setup: Artie announces Carol Burnett as a guest — she's a legend, a huge get for the final show
jokes.punchline: Larry's first instinct is to ask if she'll cry — treating her legendary status purely as an emotional prop for his farewell
jokes.explanation: Larry's emotional manipulation of his own farewell — wanting famous people to cry for him — is a perfect character reveal. 'Think she'll cry?' is delivered with the same pragmatic planning energy as casting decisions. It's Larry at his most naked: he wants the emotion, just not to feel it himself.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Don't lump me in with those fucking craft service retards

jokes.text: Larry reacts to hearing Clint Black is booked to sing to him: 'That... is a man. That's a fucking man! I don't want a fucking man singing to me!'
jokes.setup: Artie announces Clint Black as the musical guest who will sing the goodbye
jokes.punchline: Larry's objection is purely about the gender dynamic — a man singing to him — exposing his paranoid masculinity
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry masculinity panic. The escalation — 'That is a man. That's a FUCKING man!' — has a great rhythm, and the whole scene sets up the running David Duchovny/homoerotic subplot. Character-specific and sets up payoffs later.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Like wedding vows... I think you should wear a veil. I think we should come down the aisle together, maybe in white

jokes.text: Artie's defense of Clint Black: 'It's Clint! You don't have to worry about the homoerotic underpinnings. He's a country music singer.'
jokes.setup: Larry panics about a man singing to him on national TV
jokes.punchline: Artie's reassurance is the phrase 'homoerotic underpinnings' delivered as a totally normal production concern — the absurdity is in how clinical and matter-of-fact he is about it
jokes.explanation: Artie deploying 'homoerotic underpinnings' as a standard production-meeting term is genuinely funny and sharp. The follow-through — 'He's a country music singer' as if that settles it — has the exactly right Artie energy: completely rational about irrational things. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Think she'll cry?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, I didn't go so far as to make the request, but that call can be made

jokes.text: Larry: 'But a man nonetheless.'
jokes.setup: Artie assures Larry there's nothing homoerotic about Clint Black
jokes.punchline: Larry's one-line rebuttal — 'But a man nonetheless' — stands firm on the only point that matters to him
jokes.explanation: Four words that are the perfect button. The joke is in how unmovable Larry is on this point after Artie's elaborate reassurance. Economy score is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's a man. That's a fucking man! I don't want a fucking man singing to me

jokes.text: Discussion of Jim Carrey: 'We never let him plug Ace Ventura. Come on, everyone thought he was too broad. Who knew he's gonna be so—'
jokes.setup: They're discussing why Jim Carrey might be hard to book
jokes.punchline: The reveal that the show rejected Jim Carrey at his breakout moment because they thought he was 'too broad' — and the sentence trails off because hindsight makes the rest obvious
jokes.explanation: Solid industry-insider joke about late-night show snobbery toward broad comedy — and the irony that Carrey became one of the biggest stars of the era. The incomplete sentence ('who knew he's gonna be so—') is the right choice: the audience fills in the blank.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You don't have to worry about the homoerotic underpinnings. He's a country music singer

jokes.text: Someone spots Warren Beatty in the parking lot. Artie: 'He must still be putting the finishing touches on Bulworth.' Larry: 'That's already out.' Artie: 'Well, the man is never satisfied.'
jokes.setup: Warren Beatty is spotted in the parking lot, presumably near the studio
jokes.punchline: Artie's assumption that Beatty is still tweaking an already-released film, and his breezy rationalization when corrected, is a perfectly dry joke about Hollywood perfectionism/ego
jokes.explanation: 'Well, the man is never satisfied' is the ideal button — Artie doesn't miss a beat, pivoting from a factual correction to a character judgment that's both insider knowledge and completely deadpan. This is the show's comedy voice at its best: mundane, dry, and character-rich.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, that's iffy because we never let him plug Ace Ventura. Come on, everyone thought he was too broad

jokes.text: Larry approaches Warren Beatty in the parking lot, takes a deep breath, and asks if he'd like to 'come on my show tomorrow night... say a little goodbye to me.' Beatty: 'I could say goodbye to you now.' Larry: 'No, but— there are no cameras or anything here.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to recruit Beatty for the final show in an awkward parking-lot ambush
jokes.punchline: Beatty offers the perfectly logical alternative — just say goodbye now — and Larry's horrified response reveals that the goodbye is entirely for the cameras, not genuine
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Beatty's deadpan 'I could say goodbye to you now' is a genuine comic missile, and Larry's appalled 'there are no cameras or anything here' is the perfect reveal of everything the show is about — Larry's emotions only exist on television. The structure is immaculate: setup the ask, offer the logical alternative, expose the hollow truth. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Norman
dialogue.line: Hey, I think that's Warren Beatty in the parking lot. He must still be putting the finishing touches on Bulworth.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That's already out.

dialogue.speaker: Norman
dialogue.line: Well, the man is never satisfied

jokes.text: Beatty declines to appear on the show, and Larry scrambles: 'Maybe like a pretape. Let's, uh, let's think about it.'
jokes.setup: Beatty says a curt 'Goodbye' and tries to leave
jokes.punchline: Larry refuses to accept the rejection and offers a 'pretape' as a face-saving compromise — pathetically pitching it as if Beatty just needs more options
jokes.explanation: Good follow-through on the Beatty encounter. The 'pretape' offer is a nice show-business tell — Larry is still trying to produce the emotion he needs from this encounter. Solid but not as sharp as the preceding joke.

dialogue.speaker: Warren
dialogue.line: I could say goodbye to you now... There are no cameras or anything here.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Tomorrow night, millions of people

jokes.text: The discussion of David Duchovny as a replacement: 'He's a little too needy. That would be distracting for me.' / 'We believe that David's in love with Larry.'
jokes.setup: They're considering David Duchovny to replace Kevin Costner
jokes.punchline: Larry dismisses him as 'too needy' — while Artie casually states 'we believe David's in love with Larry' as a production fact, matter-of-factly
jokes.explanation: Artie delivering 'we believe that David's in love with Larry' as a logistics concern is a great line. It sets up the entire Duchovny running gag and does so efficiently. The 'needy' descriptor being Larry's primary concern (rather than the being-in-love part) is also a character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: We believe that David's in love with Larry...

dialogue.speaker: Norman
dialogue.line: He's married.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: So was Rock Hudson, ok? Oh, it wasn't real. It was arranged by the studios

jokes.text: Larry says 'He's married' as a defense. Artie: 'So was Rock Hudson, ok? Oh, it wasn't real. It was arranged by the studios.'
jokes.setup: Larry defends Duchovny's non-interest by citing his marriage
jokes.punchline: Artie invokes Rock Hudson — whose homosexuality was famously concealed — as if it's a completely standard, non-controversial industry reference point
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry-insider dark joke. Artie deploying Rock Hudson as a counter-argument — 'it was arranged by the studios' delivered with zero drama — is very much the Larry Sanders Show's register: dark, historically specific, and completely blasé. 'Oh, it wasn't real' as a quick clarification is perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He slipped on some ice making his new movie. The whole thing was all on ice or something. I don't know

jokes.text: Larry prepares to call Duchovny: 'I know his number by heart because he's a good friend of mine.' — followed by a pause as he dials
jokes.setup: Larry is about to cold-call an actor he needs as a favor
jokes.punchline: The over-explanation — 'I know his number by heart because he's a good friend of mine' — is an obvious rationalization for the intimacy of a call he's somewhat embarrassed by, given the Duchovny-is-in-love context
jokes.explanation: The self-reassurance is Larry doing his insecurity management aloud. It works because of the context — he needs to establish 'friendship' frames given what was just said about Duchovny's feelings.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I know his number by heart because he's a good friend of mine

jokes.text: David Duchovny answers the phone and immediately whispers, 'I'm glad you called. I've been thinking about you.' Then panics because his wife Téa is there and sneaks into another room.
jokes.setup: Larry calls Duchovny to ask him to appear on the show
jokes.punchline: Duchovny's first words confirm that he has in fact been thinking about Larry — and then he hides from his wife to take the call, playing it exactly like a secret affair
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Duchovny setup is excellent. The comedy is in how perfectly the actual call confirms the premise — he immediately says he's been thinking about Larry, then sneaks away from his wife to talk. It's played entirely straight, which makes it funnier. 'Shut — shut — shut the door. It's my mother. It's my mother.' is a beautiful panicked lie that deepens the joke.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: No, it's just that, uh, Téa's here... It's my mother. It's my mother

jokes.text: Duchovny sneaks into another room, closes the door, lies to Téa ('It's my mother. It's my mother.'), then answers warmly: 'Hey, how you doin'?'
jokes.setup: Duchovny is hiding from his wife to talk to Larry
jokes.punchline: The fumbling 'shut — shut — shut the door' and then the sudden warm intimacy of 'Hey, how you doin'?' — the transition from panicked deception to easy warmth is the joke
jokes.explanation: Escalates the joke from 25 nicely. The rapid-fire 'shut shut shut' then the pause and warmth plays beautifully. It's the full affair pantomime committed to by Duchovny playing himself.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm dating Illeana Douglas, as a matter of fact. She's fantastic. It's just a wonderful male-female relationship, and I am so happy

jokes.text: After Duchovny asks 'You dating anyone?', Larry says: 'I'm dating Illeana Douglas, as a matter of fact. She's fantastic. It's just a wonderful male-female relationship, and I am so happy.' Beat. Then: 'Hello?'
jokes.setup: Duchovny asks if Larry is dating anyone, seemingly fishing for information
jokes.punchline: Larry's emphatic 'wonderful male-female relationship' and 'I am so happy' is overcorrecting — stressing the heterosexuality — followed by dead silence on Duchovny's end, and then a bewildered 'Hello?'
jokes.explanation: This is the Duchovny arc's comedic peak. Larry's 'wonderful male-female relationship' is a hilariously transparent defensive maneuver — he's asserting his heterosexuality to a man who's hiding from his wife to take his call. The 'Hello?' after Duchovny's silence is the payoff: Duchovny's hurt/deflated non-response says everything. The structure is immaculate, character integration is superb, and it earns the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Meet me at the Bel-Air Hotel around noon...

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I am not meeting him at the Bel-Air. I am not meeting him...

jokes.text: Duchovny whispers the meeting location: 'Meet me at the Bel-Air Hotel around noon.' Larry immediately after hanging up: 'I am not meeting him at the Bel-Air. I am not meeting him...'
jokes.setup: Duchovny suggests lunch to discuss appearing on the show
jokes.punchline: Duchovny whispers 'the Bel-Air Hotel' as if it's a rendezvous, and Larry's flustered post-call denial ('I am not meeting him at the Bel-Air. I am not meeting him...') confirms he will absolutely go
jokes.explanation: The whispered hotel suggestion plays the tryst angle perfectly. Larry's loud protestations afterward are funny precisely because they're cut off by a knock at the door — the audience knows he'll go. A good button on the phone call sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Téa? Uh, she went golfing.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, that's fantastic.

jokes.text: Larry arrives at what is clearly the Bel-Air Hotel meeting. Duchovny: 'Téa went golfing.' Larry: 'Well, that's fantastic.'
jokes.setup: Larry said he was not meeting Duchovny at the Bel-Air — and here he is at the meeting
jokes.punchline: Duchovny volunteering that his wife is gone — with obvious implication — and Larry's enthusiastic 'Well, that's fantastic!' followed by mutual hair-complimenting is pure cringe comedy of two men trying not to acknowledge what this feels like
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Larry's denial is immediate and satisfying. Duchovny announcing Téa is out, Larry's 'that's fantastic' — and then immediately both men complimenting each other's hair — is the cringe comedy engine running at full speed. The hair compliments are the cherry on top: two heterosexual men finding the most innocent possible reason to look at each other closely.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: His behavior was so detesticle... I meant despicable

jokes.text: The two men awkwardly compliment each other's appearance: 'You look great.' 'Thank you.' 'Your hair looks great.' / 'You look great.' 'Thanks. So do you. I mean, whatever you're doing. You working out? A little bit.'
jokes.setup: Two men at a secret hotel lunch meeting after a phone call coded like an affair
jokes.punchline: They can't stop complimenting each other's looks in increasingly specific ways — the appearance-checking substituting for what the scene is actually about
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is sustained cringe rather than a single punchline — the mutual appearance-complimenting is funny because of what it implies. It's slightly overlong but the 'whatever you're doing' / 'a little bit' exchange has good texture.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Larry's a thing of the past. The guy's the 8-track. He's a fucking horse and buggy, that guy. This is Darwinism

jokes.text: Duchovny says Stevie Grant's behavior was 'detesticle.' Larry: 'Is that a word?' Duchovny: 'What'd I say?' Larry: 'You said his behavior was detesticle.' Duchovny: 'Did I? I meant despicable.'
jokes.setup: Duchovny is gossiping about a fired agent
jokes.punchline: He accidentally invents 'detesticle' — a malapropism blending 'detestable' and 'testicle' — and is genuinely confused when called on it
jokes.explanation: 'Detesticle' is one of the episode's standout comedy words — it has the ideal malapropism structure (sounds plausibly like the real word, accidentally more vulgar, and the character doesn't catch it). The beat of Larry pointing it out and Duchovny genuinely not remembering what he said is perfect. Quotability is near-10 because the word itself is memorable and repeatable. This is genuinely original wordplay that earns the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I would skip 'challenge.' Leave out 'challenge.' Do 'honor.' That's a good note, and I'll-- Tighten it up. Get to the jokes

jokes.text: Jon (the new host, replacing Larry) appears at the studio. Artie immediately starts schmoozing him: 'Monday night! Can you believe it? No. Man, I'm scared to death.' / 'I'm not blowing smoke up your ass. Larry did the show for 10 years. You're gonna do it for twice as long.'
jokes.setup: Artie is congratulating Jon on his upcoming hosting debut
jokes.punchline: Artie's shameless pivot to the new host — immediately in full producer-flattery mode — is funny given how much of the episode has been about Larry's legacy. The 'I'm not blowing smoke up your ass' line is a tell.
jokes.explanation: Artie seamlessly transferring his loyalty and flattery to the new host is character-dark comedy — the producer as eternal pragmatist. The 'twice as long' prediction is heavy compliment artillery. Solid but not transcendent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Did Stevie Grant tell you that he was signing me beforehand?

dialogue.speaker: Jon
dialogue.line: No. No, he didn't. I didn't know that.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well-- Well, well, hello, Jon

jokes.text: Artie to Jon about Larry: 'Don't worry about Larry. Ok? Larry's a thing of the past. Ok? The guy's the 8-track. He's a fucking horse and buggy, that guy. This is Darwinism. Don't fight it. You'll fucking lose.'
jokes.setup: Jon says he should probably talk to Larry before Monday
jokes.punchline: Artie dismisses Larry with the 8-track/horse and buggy double metaphor — ruthless obsolescence imagery — and frames it as evolutionary inevitability
jokes.explanation: The '8-track / horse and buggy' double-down is very good — the two different eras of obsolescence stacked together suggests Artie can't find the right metaphor because Larry is obsolete in multiple ways. 'This is Darwinism' is the killer button. Dark, ruthless, and coming from the man who has worked alongside Larry for a decade. Character integration is excellent because Artie's survival instinct is part of his DNA.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Faces from the past. They always show up for a wrapped gift

jokes.text: Larry catches Artie schmoozing Jon in the makeup room. Brief uncomfortable exchange before Artie smoothly pivots: 'Let's do the show one more time.'
jokes.setup: Larry walks in on Artie flattering his replacement
jokes.punchline: The awkward pause and Artie's pivot is the joke — Artie not even looking guilty, just smoothly transitioning as if nothing was said
jokes.explanation: The cringe of the catch is well-handled but the payoff is fairly light — 'let's do the show one more time' is a graceful save that's more poignant than funny. The comedy is mostly in the visual awkward silence rather than the lines.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I just wanted to see after you fired me and fucked up my life if you'd stand there and smile at me like we were old buddies. Well, now you know

jokes.text: Larry surveys the lobby full of people from his past. Artie: 'Faces from the past. They always show up for a wrapped gift.'
jokes.setup: The lobby is full of people Larry vaguely recognizes showing up for the final show
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'wrapped gift' line — everyone comes to the end of things for what they can get out of it — is a cynical industry observation delivered with total calm
jokes.explanation: 'They always show up for a wrapped gift' is a sharp, economical Artie line — the cynicism is baked in, and it's the kind of observation that sounds like something a veteran would genuinely say. Works as observational industry comedy with great economy.

dialogue.line: This is Martin, the sound guy you fired after he hit you in the head with a boom. 3 days in a row. Still a record

jokes.text: A woman named Darlene (apparently from India) shows up gushing: 'I'm so glad you're changing your life and leaving all of this behind and creating a new universe for yourself. It's just a big trap.' Larry: 'Thank you. Thank you so much.'
jokes.setup: Larry is greeting people from his past. Darlene appears to be some kind of spiritual/positive energy type.
jokes.punchline: She completely reframes his show as 'a big trap' that he's escaping — and Larry, to avoid conflict, just thanks her sincerely
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the collision of a spiritual world-view ('creating a new universe') with the thoroughly commercial world Larry inhabits, and his inability to push back. The 'See? He's changing already' follow-up lands it well.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I didn't realize it was the end of the show till last night. I was lying in bed with a woman, and I said, 'Seriously, we're gonna have you on soon.'

jokes.text: Jerry — who Larry fired 4 years ago — confronts him: 'Gosh, I fired you, what, 4 fucking years ago? I'll be damned.' / Jerry: 'I just wanted to see after you fired me and fucked up my life if you'd stand there and smile at me like we were old buddies.' Larry: 'Well, now you know.' Jerry: 'Yeah.' Larry: 'Huh?' Jerry: 'Huh. Nice.'
jokes.setup: Larry greets Jerry warmly, seemingly not remembering him
jokes.punchline: Jerry's confrontation is honest and earned, but Larry's response — 'Well, now you know' — delivered with cheerful unconcern, is the joke: he has no remorse and doesn't pretend to
jokes.explanation: The exchange is beautifully constructed. Jerry's confrontation is played completely straight — real grievance — and Larry's 'Well, now you know' is the ideal non-apology. The 'Huh? Huh. Nice.' coda between them is a perfectly clipped awkward pause ballet. Character integration is high because only Larry would respond to a genuine grievance with cheerful acceptance of being awful.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This show is like my sex life in that it lasts about an hour, there's applause, and I'm usually interrupted by Hank

jokes.text: Larry greets someone he doesn't remember. The man says: 'I'm happy you're here. Thank you for—' Larry trails off. Staff member: 'The lighting guy.' Larry: 'I know. I know. The lighting guy.' Another: 'The sound guy.' 'This is Martin, the sound guy you fired after he hit you in the head with a boom. 3 days in a row. Still a record.'
jokes.setup: Larry is introduced to someone he doesn't recognize, struggling to place them
jokes.punchline: The escalation: lighting guy → sound guy who hit Larry with a boom mic → THREE DAYS IN A ROW → 'still a record.' Each beat is funnier than the last.
jokes.explanation: 'Still a record' is the perfect button. The escalation structure is textbook — each revelation is more absurd than the last, culminating in the boom mic hitting being a three-day repeating offense turned into a workplace statistic. The structure score is high because the escalation is controlled and each step earns the next. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: When we started this show 10 years ago, Michael Jackson still looked like Michael Jackson

jokes.text: 'Screw you, Larry.' 'Yeah, screw you.' — The sound guy and another ex-employee, barely missing a beat after the laugh
jokes.setup: The 'still a record' revelation ends with Larry laughing good-naturedly
jokes.punchline: The two former employees casually tell Larry to screw himself — not angry, just matter-of-fact — and walk away
jokes.explanation: Good button on the sequence. The casual dual 'screw you' has nice rhythm and the understatement works — not a dramatic confrontation, just a small transaction of resentment. Economy is the strength here.

dialogue.speaker: Greg Kinnear
dialogue.line: I'm acting now... It's a snap. One minute I'm talking to Tempestt Bledsoe at 1:35 in the morning about her dogs or something, next thing you know I got a nomination

jokes.text: 'Sid's brother. Hi.'
jokes.setup: Larry is meeting a parade of faces from the past, each with a backstory
jokes.punchline: This guest has no story — he's just 'Sid's brother' — the utterly bathetic endpoint of the montage
jokes.explanation: 'Sid's brother. Hi.' is comedy through pure economy and anti-climax. After the lightning-bolt reunion with Jerry and the boom-mic escalation, this is two words and a greeting. The comedy is structural — the sudden deflation after escalation. Economy score is 10 because it literally cannot be shorter.

dialogue.speaker: Jim Carrey
dialogue.line: I can't do comedy right now... You're leaving, Larry. Just when I thought everything was solid in my life... You decide to go

jokes.text: Larry asks if there are more people from the past outside. Then: 'No, but I got a present for you. The great Jim Carrey is in the house.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been through an ordeal of awkward reunions and asks if it's over
jokes.punchline: The reassurance ('no more people from the past') is immediately followed by an even bigger incoming disruption: Jim Carrey
jokes.explanation: A functional transitional joke. The misdirection (no more people from the past → Jim Carrey) is mild. Works more as scene setup than a strong comedic moment.

dialogue.speaker: Jim Carrey
dialogue.line: I can't get it up. Ever since the announcement, I've been flaccid

jokes.text: Larry on air: 'I didn't realize it was the end of the show till last night. I was lying in bed with a woman, and I said, 'Seriously, we're gonna have you on soon.' Now I'm in trouble.'
jokes.setup: Larry is doing his monologue, reminiscing about the end of the show
jokes.punchline: He reveals mid-sex pillow talk he was still booking guests — the show consumed his personal life so completely he was promising airtime to someone in bed
jokes.explanation: This is a great Larry monologue joke — the show is his entire identity, so completely that it invades his intimate life. 'Seriously, we're gonna have you on soon' as pillow talk is a terrific image. The 'now I'm in trouble' button is perfectly understated. Character integration is excellent: this joke could only work with Larry as the subject.

dialogue.speaker: Jim Carrey
dialogue.line: The elaborate 'No Way' chant and song performance

jokes.text: Larry: 'We just installed the sound system today.' Beat. 'I didn't realize it was the end of the show till last night.'
jokes.setup: Larry opens the final show and asks if the audience can hear him OK.
jokes.punchline: The double punchline: new sound system installed today (absurd last-minute preparation), plus Larry claims he didn't know the show was ending until last night — delivered completely deadpan.
jokes.explanation: Two-part monologue joke. The sound system line is surreal production commentary; the 'didn't know it was ending till last night' is deliberate anti-sentimentality. Both work individually; the pairing is efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Jim Carrey
dialogue.line: Let's just cut the crap, Larry. You never liked my work. Till I got hugely famous

jokes.text: Larry's monologue: 'I was lying in bed with a woman, and I said, 'Seriously, we're gonna have you on soon.' Now I'm in trouble.'
jokes.setup: Larry says he only realized this was the last show last night, while in bed with a woman
jokes.punchline: He was apparently booking the final show while in bed with a guest — and now he's going to have to make good on it
jokes.explanation: A sharp, self-contained monologue joke that captures Larry's total inability to separate his personal and professional life. The idea that he was in bed promising TV appearances is simultaneously plausible and absurd. 'Now I'm in trouble' is a perfectly dry punchline. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jim Carrey
dialogue.line: Let's just cut the crap, Larry. Ok? You never liked my work. Huh? Till I got hugely famous.

jokes.text: 'Because the show, oddly, is like my sex life in that it lasts about an hour, there's applause, and I'm usually interrupted by Hank.'
jokes.setup: Larry is riffing on how the show is 'oddly' like something
jokes.punchline: The three-part parallel ('lasts about an hour, there's applause, I'm interrupted by Hank') turns sex comparison into a Hank joke — the third element is the subversive turn
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best constructed jokes. The rule-of-three structure is textbook: first two comparisons set up the sex parallel, third element is the pivot to Hank that recontextualizes the whole thing as a Larry/Hank relationship joke. 'Interrupted by Hank' landing on the sex-life list is the exact right surprise. Highly quotable, excellent structure. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Jim Carrey
dialogue.line: I'm here for 3 good reasons. Last show, big ratings, movie coming out. Bim, bam, boom. Otherwise, I'd be sitting home watching Nightline

jokes.text: Larry: 'Oddly enough, Clinton is our first 2-intern president.'
jokes.setup: Larry is riffing about the show surviving 3 presidential administrations
jokes.punchline: '2-intern president' is a compressed, original formulation of the Clinton/Lewinsky scandal
jokes.explanation: '2-intern president' is a clever compression — it's the kind of political joke that works because it's efficient and original in its framing rather than just referencing the scandal. Economy is near-perfect. Loses points on character integration because it could work from any late-night host at the time.

dialogue.speaker: Clint Black
dialogue.line: For what, Talk Soup?

jokes.text: 'Do you realize when we started this show 10 years ago, Michael Jackson still looked like Michael Jackson?'
jokes.setup: Larry is cataloguing what has changed over the show's 10-year run
jokes.punchline: Michael Jackson's appearance change is framed as a historical marker on par with presidential administrations — the absurdity is in the equivalence
jokes.explanation: Functional celebrity observation joke. The framing as historical marker is clever, but this type of joke was common in late-night at the time. Economy is its strength.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Petty
dialogue.line: I haven't seen such a rumble since the Stones played Altamont

jokes.text: Greg Kinnear's exchange: Larry asks about his talk show, Kinnear says 'I'm acting now.' Larry: 'Really?' Kinnear: 'Yeah, I, uh, I got an academy award nomination.' Larry: 'You're acting?' Kinnear: 'Yeah, I mean, it's a snap. One minute I'm talking to Tempestt Bledsoe at 1:35 in the morning about her dogs or something, next thing you know I got a nomination. It's like...' Larry: 'God bless you.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks Kinnear about his talk show, expecting industry small talk
jokes.punchline: Kinnear got an Oscar nomination for acting — which he describes as 'a snap' — specifically by pivoting away from late-night. The implicit insult to Larry (who never pivoted) is sharpened by Larry's repeated 'You're acting?' disbelief, and Kinnear's specificity about the banality of talk show booking (Tempestt Bledsoe, dogs, 1:35 AM)
jokes.explanation: This joke works on multiple levels: it's a real-world reference (Kinnear was actually nominated for As Good As It Gets), an implicit critique of the talk show format, and a subtle knife in Larry at the end of his run. 'Tempestt Bledsoe at 1:35 in the morning about her dogs' is a perfect specificity — the soul-crushing grind of late-night booking compressed into one image. 'God bless you' as Larry's non-response is the right button.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Petty
dialogue.line: I haven't seen such a rumble since the Stones played Altamont.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Bob, is that all we have on the cards? After all these years, we're out of cards, so we'll be right back.'
jokes.setup: Larry is mid-monologue, apparently running out of material
jokes.punchline: He breaks the fourth wall on the machinery of the show — running out of index cards — and treats it as a perfectly normal wrap-up
jokes.explanation: A nice meta moment — the show's own production apparatus exposed on its final night. 'After all these years, we're out of cards' has a dry poignancy that functions as both a joke and a valedictory beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Petty
dialogue.line: You've already got Roy Rogers.

jokes.text: 'We'll be right back. No flipping.'
jokes.setup: Standard commercial break send-off
jokes.punchline: 'No flipping' — the show's famous catchphrase, used on the actual final show — is both in-joke and valedictory, a tiny perfect button
jokes.explanation: 'No flipping' is the show's signature line — its use here on the final show is emotionally loaded and metacomically resonant. Two words that carry the weight of the entire series. Economy is perfect (10). Quotability is high for fans.

jokes.text: Jim Carrey enters to a massive ovation and immediately begins performing for the audience without waiting for Larry: 'You'd think it was your last night.'
jokes.setup: Jim Carrey is introduced and the audience goes wild
jokes.punchline: Carrey's first line to Larry — 'You'd think it was your last night' — is delivered with mock surprise, as if he's noticing the fuss for the first time
jokes.explanation: A neat entrance line — the mock-obliviousness of 'you'd think it was your last night' while performing at the actual last night is a clean ironic joke. Simple and effective.

jokes.text: Jim Carrey lauding Larry: '...to go out when you're at the very tip top of your game. The cream of the crop. King of the hill. Cock of the walk!'
jokes.setup: Carrey is praising Larry with increasing enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: 'Cock of the walk' is the escalation that breaks decorum — each phrase is progressively more intense until it tips into the accidental double entendre
jokes.explanation: Carrey playing a heightened version of himself — over-enthused, escalating to absurdity — fits perfectly. 'Cock of the walk' lands with the right awkward energy, and Larry's 'I know walk is certainly correct' is a great dry follow-up.

jokes.text: Larry responds to 'Cock of the walk': 'That is so kind. I know walk is certainly correct.'
jokes.setup: Carrey has just said 'cock of the walk' with full energy
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat, precise parsing — acknowledging only the 'walk' part — is perfect deadpan. The implicit acknowledgment that the 'cock' part is debatable (or that he heard it) is the subtext
jokes.explanation: Larry's response is a miniature masterpiece of deadpan. By isolating and approving only 'walk,' he simultaneously acknowledges the crude word and deflects it while maintaining total composure. It's the kind of line that reveals everything about a character in six words. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Carrey starts telling the story of the Newhart finale — then trails off into a long, painful, incoherent non-description: 'When, uh — when, uh... Bob goes back and has the dream... they do kind of a — uh... it's almost like they're, uh... Just right in the...'
jokes.setup: Carrey is enthusiastically referencing the famous Newhart finale to make a point
jokes.punchline: He cannot describe it — the story completely collapses mid-sentence. The increasingly long pauses and vague gestures are the comedy
jokes.explanation: A sustained awkward-pause joke that works because of Carrey's specific brand of manic commitment — even when he's lost, he keeps going. The audience watches him spin out in real time. The failure IS the joke, which is a character-integrated choice: Carrey can't do subtle.

jokes.text: 'I'm sor — I can't do this. I can't do comedy right now.'
jokes.setup: Carrey has just failed to describe the Newhart finale on live TV
jokes.punchline: 'I can't do comedy right now' — spoken on live television during a comedy show — is a funny meta confession, and it sets up his emotional breakdown
jokes.explanation: The line works as a transitional joke before the full breakdown — Carrey is aware enough to announce his own failure, which is itself a bit. The meta element (comedian saying he can't do comedy) is clean.

jokes.text: Carrey's breakdown: 'You're leaving, Larry. Just when I thought everything was solid in my life... you decide to go. You know, I can't get it up.' (pause) 'Ever since the announcement, I've been flaccid.'
jokes.setup: Carrey is delivering what appears to be a heartfelt emotional speech about Larry leaving
jokes.punchline: 'I can't get it up' followed by 'Ever since the announcement, I've been flaccid' — he's describing sexual dysfunction caused by Larry's retirement, playing the parasocial bond as a literal physiological condition
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The setup is a genuine emotional speech — 'just when I thought everything was solid in my life' — which makes the pivot to sexual dysfunction funnier. 'Ever since the announcement, I've been flaccid' is a highly quotable, specific, and original line. It also plays as a callback to the episode's running theme of men's weird intimacy with Larry. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Carrey: 'I'm sure everyone in this audience feels the same way.' — then rallies the audience with 'No Way!' chants
jokes.setup: Carrey has just confessed to erectile dysfunction caused by Larry leaving
jokes.punchline: He generalizes his sexual dysfunction to the entire audience — 'I'm sure everyone feels the same way' — as if mass flaccidity is the expected response to the show ending
jokes.explanation: The generalization of personal dysfunction to the audience is a good escalation beat. The 'No Way!' rally that follows is Carrey at his most unhinged, which is exactly right for the character-as-himself comedy.

jokes.text: Carrey launches into a full performance of 'No Way' — improvised song with the audience, escalating to a Jennifer Holliday 'And I Am Telling You' pastiche, complete with screaming
jokes.setup: What starts as Carrey rallying the audience against Larry's departure becomes a full musical performance
jokes.punchline: The escalation to 'And I Am Telling You' parody (a song of romantic desperation) applied to a talk show host's retirement is the joke — the disproportionate emotional artillery
jokes.explanation: The extended Carrey musical performance is big, physical, and escalating. It's Jim Carrey 1998 at maximum volume — playing himself as a force of nature. The joke is the concept (Jennifer Holliday about a late-night show cancellation) and the execution is in his commitment. Economy is lower because the bit runs long, but the impact in the room would be high.

jokes.text: Carrey to Larry backstage: 'Let's cut the crap, Larry. Ok? You never liked my work. Huh? Till I got hugely famous.'
jokes.setup: Larry is gushing about how fantastic the Carrey performance was
jokes.punchline: Carrey drops the persona and goes fully real: 'You never liked my work till I got hugely famous' — a direct accusation that punctures all the warmth
jokes.explanation: The pivot from the massive performance to cold confrontation is a great structural move. Carrey's accusation is a direct callback to the earlier revelation that the show rejected him for being 'too broad.' The cringe comedy of Larry trying to maintain the warmth while Carrey is done with pretense is excellent.

jokes.text: Carrey: 'What are you gonna do now? Movies?' Larry: 'I'll crush you.' Carrey: 'I— are you doing a bit now?' Larry: 'Larry... [whispers] We're off the air. This is real life now.'
jokes.setup: Carrey asks what Larry's career plans are
jokes.punchline: 'I'll crush you' — Larry's competitive instinct overrides his farewell dignity. Then 'are you doing a bit?' is Carrey genuinely confused whether it's a joke, and Larry's 'This is real life now' confirms his delusion
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. 'I'll crush you' is a perfect character moment — Larry's competitive paranoia erupting at the worst possible time. But the structure is what elevates it: Carrey's 'are you doing a bit?' is an outsider's genuine bewilderment, and Larry's earnest 'this is real life now' is devastating. It reveals Larry is performing even when he thinks he's being real. Character integration is as high as it gets — this joke could not exist with any other character. Justifies 9+ on impact.

jokes.text: Carrey: 'What are you gonna do now? Movies? I'll crush you.'
jokes.setup: Carrey is now fully in confrontational mode with Larry
jokes.punchline: 'I'll crush you' — delivered with the calm confidence of someone stating a fact, not making a threat
jokes.explanation: Maximally economical and totally in character for how Jim Carrey is being written here. The casual matter-of-factness of 'I'll crush you' — not as a boast but as a prediction — is both funny and a little chilling. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Are you doing a bit now?' / Carrey: '[Whispers] We're off the air. This is real life now.'
jokes.setup: Larry, off-camera, tries to determine if Carrey's hostility is performance or real
jokes.punchline: Carrey whispers 'We're off the air. This is real life now.' — the meta-invocation of the show's central tension between performance and reality
jokes.explanation: A thematically rich joke. 'This is real life now' is the Larry Sanders show's central anxiety made explicit — where does the performance end? The whisper delivery adds menace. The joke works as character comedy (Larry can't tell if anyone is performing) and as meta-commentary on the show's themes.

jokes.text: Carrey: 'I'm here for 3 good reasons. Last show, big ratings, movie coming out. Bim, bam, boom. Otherwise, I'd be sitting home and watching Nightline. As usual.'
jokes.setup: Carrey just dropped the warm persona backstage; he now explains why he's really there
jokes.punchline: 'Bim, bam, boom. Otherwise I'd be sitting home and watching Nightline. As usual.' — the brutal honesty about celebrity appearances (pure self-promotion) undercut by the pathetic 'as usual' suggesting he's actually home alone every night
jokes.explanation: 'Bim, bam, boom' is terrific rhythm. The structural move — ruthless honesty about Hollywood self-promotion — is good on its own, but 'As usual' is the surprise element that adds depth: the most famous comedian in the world watching Nightline alone. It humanizes while deflating. 'As usual' does enormous work in two words. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Clint Black: 'I thought I was your Bette Midler. This is bullshit.' — then to Artie: 'Those were your exact words.'
jokes.setup: There's an argument backstage about who gets to sing the goodbye song
jokes.punchline: Country singer Clint Black insisting he was promised the role of 'your Bette Midler' — the specific reference, the indignation, and Artie apparently having made that promise
jokes.explanation: 'I thought I was your Bette Midler' from Clint Black is genuinely great — the specific absurdity of a male country singer claiming the Bette Midler role for a man he barely knows is perfectly ridiculous. It also callbacks Larry's 'I don't want a man singing to me' worry and suggests Artie has been making incompatible promises to everyone. High quotability.

jokes.text: Clint Black confronts Artie: 'Hey, I don't know what you're telling him, but you told me that I was doing the good-bye song.' / Artie: 'Quiet down, cowpoke.'
jokes.setup: Artie is managing a conflict backstage between multiple guests who think they're doing the farewell song
jokes.punchline: Artie dismisses a country music star's legitimate grievance with 'Quiet down, cowpoke' — a perfectly condescending, genre-specific put-down
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'Quiet down, cowpoke' is a gem — it's dismissive, genre-specific (calling a country singer 'cowpoke' is both accurate and condescending), and delivered with Artie's signature lack of apology. The economy is near-perfect. A very quotable Artie line that earns its place among the episode's best.

jokes.text: Artie to Clint Black: 'Quiet down, cowpoke. I'm talking to Artie.'
jokes.setup: Clint Black is confronting Artie about the goodbye song promise
jokes.punchline: 'Quiet down, cowpoke' — Artie manages the situation with total calm, deploying a Western idiom that both acknowledges Clint Black's genre and dismisses him
jokes.explanation: 'Cowpoke' is the perfect dismissive register for Artie — condescending but culturally on-point for addressing a country singer. Maximum economy, totally in character for the unflappable producer.

jokes.text: Greg Kinnear scoffs at Clint Black: 'For what, Talk Soup?' — then gets physically restrained: 'Greg, no!'
jokes.setup: Jim Carrey defends Kinnear by citing his Oscar nomination; Clint Black dismisses it
jokes.punchline: 'For what, Talk Soup?' — Clint Black (or someone) dismisses Kinnear's Oscar nom as being for his talk show roots — and then the physical escalation ('Greg, no!') suggests Kinnear nearly attacks someone over it
jokes.explanation: 'For what, Talk Soup?' is a satisfying diss that's also an industry insider joke — Kinnear was known for Talk Soup before transitioning to film. The Greg-nearly-attacking-someone beat escalates the chaos appropriately.

jokes.text: Artie, watching backstage chaos: 'I haven't seen such a rumble since the Stones played Altamont.'
jokes.setup: Celebrities are about to come to blows backstage
jokes.punchline: Artie's historical frame of reference — comparing a backstage green room scuffle to Altamont (where a man was killed by Hell's Angels at a Rolling Stones concert) — is so disproportionate it's perfect
jokes.explanation: Artie's Altamont reference is quintessential Artie — drawing on a decade older than everyone else in the room, making a disproportionate comparison with total calm. 'I haven't seen such a rumble since the Stones played Altamont' is the kind of line that gets better the more you think about it. The specificity (not just 'a Stones concert' but 'Altamont') elevates it. High quotability, justified 8+.

jokes.text: The scene erupts: 'Kick his ass! Kick his ass!' then 'Whoa, whoa, whoa!' and everyone shouting
jokes.setup: Backstage chaos has been building with multiple celebrity conflicts
jokes.punchline: The chaos reaches full mob energy — 'Kick his ass!' being shouted at what is essentially a TV green room — the absurd extremity of Hollywood ego battles
jokes.explanation: The closing chaos is more of a structural payoff than a specific joke — the accumulated absurdity of the episode exploding. It's earned but not particularly clever in itself. Functions as an episode closer rather than a standout comedic moment.

tmdb_overview: Larry scrambles to get his last show together, and must confront David Duchovny's affections in order to secure him as a guest. Arthur tries to keep the staff's emotions together as things are packed up and the last show is done.
